title.en: How nature works in harmony: habitats, ecosystems and the elephant corridor

text.en: In states like Odisha, Jharkhand and Assam, elephants wander into farms when forests shrink and waterholes dry up. A corridor of forest linking two reserves can help them move safely.

A habitat is the place where an organism lives, and it can be as small as the bark of a tree.
Plants and animals living in a habitat together with non-living things like soil, water and air form an ecosystem.
Producers like green plants make food by photosynthesis, consumers eat other organisms, and decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead matter.
A food chain shows who eats whom, such as grass → deer → tiger, and many food chains join into a food web.
Energy flows from the Sun through producers to consumers, and most of it is lost as heat at every step.
Nutrients are recycled by decomposers, so nothing in nature is truly wasted.
Removing even one species can disturb the whole web, so biodiversity (the variety of life) keeps nature stable.
Forest loss, roads, farms and mining break habitats apart, so animals lose food and routes.
A wildlife corridor is a strip of habitat that links two forests, letting animals like elephants move without entering villages.
We can protect nature through reserves, corridors, afforestation and by saving water and avoiding waste.

problem.en: Write a food chain from a pond and name each member's role.

text.en: Algae are producers and fish are consumers.

requiredIdeas.en: They search for food and water.

points.en: An ecosystem has living and non-living parts.
Producers, consumers and decomposers keep energy and nutrients moving.
Biodiversity and corridors keep nature in balance.
